TRANSCRIPT OF PROCEEDINGS
THE HON CATHERINE HOLMES AC SC, Commissioner
THE ROYAL COMMISSION INTO THE ROBODEBT SCHEME
THURSDAY, 3 NOVEMBER 2022 AT 10.05 AM (AEST)
DAY 6
MR JUSTIN GREGGERY KC, Senior Counsel Assisting
MR ANGUS SCOTT, Counsel Assisting
MS SALWA MARSH, Counsel Assisting
MS DOMINIQUE HOGAN-DORAN SC, for the Commonwealth
MR TRENT GLOVER, for the Commonwealth
MR A VIAL, for the Commonwealth

COMMISSIONER: Yes, appearances for the day, please.
MR SCOTT: Commissioner, if the Commission pleases, Scott, initials AD, is my name. I will be
appearing to assist the Commission with respect to the first two witnesses, Mr Brown and
Ms Keeling. Mr Greggery with Ms Marsh will appear to assist the Commission with respect
to Mr Hirschhorn.
COMMISSIONER: Thank you. Ms Hogan-Doran?
MS HOGAN-DORAN: Commissioner, I appear today with Mr Glover and Mr Vial of Counsel
for the Commonwealth.
COMMISSIONER: Yes, Mr Scott
MR SCOTT: Before the hearing commences, I understand Ms Hogan-Doran has a matter to
raise.
COMMISSIONER: Yes, Ms Hogan-Doran.
MS HOGAN-DORAN: Thank you, Commissioner. Commissioner, I have ascertained an issue
as to witness access to classified emails - the Commonwealth witnesses. I can confirm to you
that Mr Jones who was called to give evidence - is it yesterday?
COMMISSIONER: It blurs, but I think it might have been the day before.
MS HOGAN-DORAN: Mr Jones and Mr Brown have both been given access to their classified
and unclassified emails for the purpose of them giving evidence. That is, they have had
access to all relevant material. However, Ms Keeling, who is on today's witness list, has not
been granted access to her secure emails. I have conferred with Counsel Assisting and I have
spoken with the witness. The evidence that she is being called to give today, I understand, is
unlikely to be affected by that limited access, but that her future evidence may be, and that
will be taken up post this hearing.
COMMISSIONER: Just explain to me, how does it work? Who makes these decisions?
MS HOGAN-DORAN: Commissioner, I'm seeking urgent instructions confirming how that has
occurred.
COMMISSIONER: I don't suppose it's malice but it's certainly obstructive.
MS HOGAN-DORAN: Commissioner, I can't assist you in either respect. I don't know of
anything at this point that would indicate in any way that it is malicious.
COMMISSIONER: No. And as I say, I'm not suggesting that for a moment, but it sounds like
the bureaucracy has gone a bit mad in a way that has the potential to interfere with the

functions of this inquiry and something that needs remedying. And I'm assuming it's the
bureaucracy.
MS HOGAN-DORAN: Commissioner, I think - I will start that again. Commissioner, as I
understand it, is that only affected witnesses who were previously officials of the
Commonwealth who had to have material made available to and it had to be produced to
them for the purposes of them providing their statements. The witnesses we have seen
already, that is, Mr Jones and now Mr Brown are both former officials at the relevant
Department. It's the logistics of that material being extracted and provided to those
witnesses that I apprehend is the issue.
I have sought in the last two days to remedy that in respect of those witnesses as they have
come on. Ms Keeling - and got to Ms Keeling, I understand that it may not - that's all I wish
to say about those three witnesses. There are no additional witnesses this week that it
would affect, and I'm having the position urgently reviewed in respect of any witnesses next
week.
COMMISSIONER: That's all very consistent with your very cooperative attitude,
Ms Hogan-Doran, and I'm grateful
MS HOGAN-DORAN: Thank you, Commissioner.
COMMISSIONER: Thank you. Yes, Mr Scott.
MR SCOTT: Just one further matter of housekeeping, Commissioner. I don't anticipate this
witness and Ms Keeling to take more than a bit over an hour, but perhaps that's sufficient
for Mr Hirschhorn to give a not before time of 11.
COMMISSIONER: Certainly. 11 o'clock.
MR SCOTT: Thank you, Commissioner.
COMMISSIONER: If we do get some idle minutes anywhere, I still have a ruling to give, so we
can probably do that somewhere before the line. Thank you.
MR SCOTT: In that case, Commissioner, I call Cameron Brown.
COMMISSIONER: Yes. Mr Brown, an oath or an affirmation?
MR BROWN: Affirmation please, Commissioner.
COMMISSIONER: Thank you.
ASSOCIATE: The response will be I do. Do you solemnly declare and affirm that the evidence
you will give will be the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth?

<CAMERON ARTHUR BROWN, AFFIRMED
<EXAMINATION BY MR SCOTT
COMMISSIONER: Thank you. Mr Scott.
MR SCOTT: Thank you Commissioner. Mr Brown, could you please tell the Commission your
full name?
MR BROWN: Cameron Arthur Brown.
MR SCOTT: It's the case, isn't it, that you received a notice to give a statement from the
Commission?
MR BROWN: Yes, it is.
MR SCOTT: And to produce documents relevant to that statement?
MR BROWN: Yes, it is.
MR SCOTT: You provided a statement in response to that notice dated 27 October 2022?
MR BROWN: Yes, I provided a statement. There are minor amendments to the statement
which has arisen following looking at my email records.
MR SCOTT: Can you please, with reference to the paragraphs in your statement, just identify
the corrections you wish to make?
MR BROWN: Yes, paragraph 10, where it reads:
"From about December 2013 to approximately 23 November...”
That 23 November should read 17 November. At the end of that paragraph, I would also like
to state that I took leave between 16 and 23 October 2014. In paragraph 11, where it begins
"On or about 23 November", that 23 should read 17 November. At the end of that line, in
paragraph 11, where it reads "on 23 November 2014", it should "on 17 November." On - in
paragraph 13, in the final line, where the final sentence is:
"I did not return to the DSS in any capacity after 23 November."
It should read "17 November.” In paragraph 23, where the paragraph begins:
"Between 1 October 2014 to approximately 23 November..."
It should read "17 November." And at the end of that paragraph, it should read:

"In addition, I took leave between 16 and 23 October 2014."
And they are all the corrections. Or amendments.
MR SCOTT: Thank you, Mr Brown. Is the statement otherwise true and correct to the best of
your knowledge and belief?
MR BROWN: Yes, it is.
MR SCOTT: Thank you. Commissioner, I tender Mr Brown's statement and notice, and hand
up a list of documents for tender today.
COMMISSIONER: Thank you. And you have given a copy to Ms Hogan-Doran?
MR SCOTT: I believe it's been provided.
MS HOGAN-DORAN: I do, Commissioner. I would ask my friend just to confine his tender at
this stage to the evidence of Mr Brown and not the balance of the documents. There is an
issue in relation to one later in the day.
COMMISSIONER: Alright. Well, I will admit the statement and the notice and the compliance
measure document and some record of a conversation between Mr Jones and Brown, and
they will be exhibits 152 to 155 in the sequence on the schedule.
<EXHIBITS 152 TO 155 STATEMENT OF CAMERON BROWN DATED 27/10/2022, NOTICE,
COMPLIANCE MEASURE DOCUMENT, RECORD OF CONVERSATION BETWEEN MR JONES
AND MR BROWN
MR SCOTT: Thank you, Commissioner.
MS HOGAN-DORAN: Sorry, Commissioner, the list I have begins at 151 and Mr Brown's
evidence finishes at 154. Are we adding one number from yesterday?
COMMISSIONER: I imagine that's the case. Yes. That is correct, Ms Hogan-Doran, I'm told by
my associate.
MS HOGAN-DORAN: Thank you.
MR SCOTT: Mr Brown, is it the case that since preparing this statement - your
statement - you have identified further documents relevant to your statement and provided
them to the Australian Government Solicitor?
MR BROWN: Yes, that is correct. I have had a chance on Monday and yesterday to look
through some of my email records. I would note that I had - the emails which were provided
to me were not complete. There was a small selection on Monday. Further emails were
provided to me yesterday morning. They were not complete. There was a missing month.

actually probably the key month in question, which is over October - you know,
October/November. I would just like to make the statement that I am not fully confident
that I have seen all of my emails, given the difficulty in retrieving them from the archives
and their incomplete nature when they have been provided.
MR SCOTT: When you say or refer to emails that have been provided to you, provided to
you by whom?
MR BROWN: I - they are provided to me by the support staff here at AGD and AGS, and I
assume they come from DSS.
MR SCOTT: And how are you satisfied - how do you satisfy yourself as to the inquiries that
are made by those support staff to identify relevant documents?
COMMISSIONER: Or does he satisfy himself? It doesn't sound as if he does.
MR SCOTT: Yes.
MR BROWN: Well, I can't. I don't have any means of doing that.
MR SCOTT: So, in other words, are you entirely reliant upon the support staff that you refer
to identify relevant documents?
MR BROWN: Not to identify - I've gone through my emails to identify the relevant
documents, but is that a complete sort of library of my documents? That's what I
can't - that's what I am not able to satisfy myself in regard to. I don't have access. I no longer
work at the Department of Social Services. So I don't have any personal access to that,
which Senior Counsel raised earlier.
MR SCOTT: Mr Brown, are you prepared, if given the opportunity, to review any further
documents and if any further relevant documents are identified to provide them to the
Commission?
MR BROWN: Yes, I am.
MR SCOTT: Thank you, Mr Brown. So if I could just come back to those further documents
that you have identified since preparing your statement.
MR BROWN: Yes.
MR SCOTT: Do you have a bundle of those documents in front of you with an index to them
numbered - with documents numbered 1 to 8?
MR BROWN: Yes, I do.

MR SCOTT: Commissioner, some of these documents are already before the Commission
and have gone into evidence, some haven't. But I do have a copy of the bundle with the
schedule which I can hand up so you can follow this evidence.
COMMISSIONER: Thank you.
MR SCOTT: I should say, the bundle with the index been provided to me by legal
representatives for the Commonwealth. So apart from your statement - I assume you've got
your statement in front of you there, Mr Brown?
MR BROWN: Yes, I do.
MR SCOTT: The documents referred to in your statement and the additional documents we
just discussed, do you have any other documents before you that you are referring to?
MR BROWN: No, I just have those documents just printed out for ease of reference.
MR SCOTT: Okay. Thank you, Mr Brown. Now you are presently the Acting Assistant
Secretary of the Health branch of Department of Finance?
MR BROWN: Yes, that's correct.
MR SCOTT: You’ve held this role since about 18 October 2022?
MR BROWN: Yes.
MR SCOTT: And noting the corrections to your statement earlier, previously you were a
Director or the Director of Payment Integrity and Debt Management in the Department of
Social Services from about December 2013 to approximately 17 November 2014?
MR BROWN: That is correct.
MR SCOTT: And you reported in that role to someone called Murray Kimber, the Assistant
Secretary of the Department?
MR BROWN: Yes, that is correct.
MR SCOTT: And at various points in your employment in that capacity, you acted as
Assistant Secretary of DSS when Mr Kimber was on leave?
MR BROWN: Yes, so I recall acting for short times when Mr Kimber went on leave.
MR SCOTT: Thank you. Could you just turn to paragraph 29 of your statement, please? And
could that be brought up on the screen? If we can call out that paragraph. Now, you say
there that while you were employed with DSS, the general practice of the DSA was that:

"When a proposal was raised by stakeholder that might affect security law, internal legal
advice was sought to ensure that the proposal accorded with law. Where the DSS received
internal legal advice that a particular proposal was not consistent with the law, it would rely
on the advice to push back on the proposal. If the legal advice supported the DSS's
opposition to an idea, there would have been a greater justification to push back on the
idea.”
Do you see that?
MR BROWN: Yes.
MR SCOTT: Are you - when you in that paragraph use the term "proposal", are you meaning
to refer to what's known as a new policy proposal or the word "proposal" in a different
sense?
MR BROWN: I'm referring to it in a broader sense which would also encompass new policy
proposals. However, in that sense, it's - any idea which was presented to the Department,
we would - if it affected security law, we would then seek advice from our legal area as to
how that accorded with the law.
MR SCOTT: Just to assist the Commission in a definitional sense, the term "new policy
proposal", that has obviously a particular significance within the Commonwealth, doesn't it?
MR BROWN: Yes, it does. It has a formal - really a formal meeting - meaning, sorry, which is
really the vehicle through which the new policy proposal, if it was to proceed, would be
attached to a cabinet submission and that cabinet submission would then go to cabinet for
consideration. In particular, it would go to the Expenditure Review Committee of cabinet
and that would be the document upon which they would rely to make a determination as to
whether it proceeds.
MR SCOTT: Thank you. Now, you recall in mid to late 2014, DHS, the Department of Human
Services, raised a proposal with DSS, the Department of Social Services, involving a process
known as income smoothing to calculate debts owed to the Commonwealth by social
security recipients. Do you recall that?
MR BROWN: Yes, I do.
MR SCOTT: Do you recall how you became aware of that proposal?
MR BROWN: I believe, to the best of my recollection, that initially it was raised verbally in a
meeting and then further detail was sought over the ensuing weeks or potentially months. I
don't have a clear recollection of precisely when it was first raised. However, I can see from
the ensuing emails that we must have received more detail in regard to it. However, I have
not been able to find in my email an actual sort of written submission or email from DHS to
DSS saying "Well, this is what it is." That may have been determined verbally through
contact between my staff and DHS, however, I - there is no - I cannot find a document to

MR SCOTT: Okay. Do you recall who first raised it with you?
MR BROWN: I - from my recollection, it was - I do not recall who raised it with me. I know
who it was probably likely, and that is Mr Mark Withnell the First Assistant Secretary, who
we were dealing with, or it was potentially Scott Britton, who was I think the Assistant
Secretary at DHS. However, I am not 100 per cent certain of that.
MR SCOTT: When you say Mr Withnell was the person you were dealing with, in what
capacity were you dealing with Mr Withnell?
MR BROWN: We had regular or semiregular meetings with our counterparts at DHS to
discuss ongoing issues. There were a number of sort of major pieces of work which were
proceeding over the course of 2014, not least of which was the negotiation of a new
performance agreement framework between the Department of Social Services and DHS.
That framework I'm happy to go into more detail about. However, in answer to your
question those meetings were, as I said, regular. I remember Mr Withnell and Mr Britton
attending. Certainly Mr Kimber on our side attended. And I recall Ms Foster, my First
Assistant Secretary, attending those meetings on occasion as well.
MR SCOTT: Okay. Now, income smoothing is a process involving an assumption that a social
security recipient earns the same amount of income for each fortnight that they are in
receipt of a benefit, correct?
MR BROWN: Yes. Income smoothing is where you know how much they earn over an
extended period of time and then you apportion it equally into fortnightly allotments across
that period of time.
MR SCOTT: And it would be right, wouldn't it, that for many recipients of social security, that
assumption, in reality, would be wrong; correct?
MR BROWN: Yes, that's correct. Those with variable income, such as casuals, shift workers,
people who undertook loading - you know, so, like, overtime, etcetera - that would be
wrong.
MR SCOTT: And it would be right, wouldn't it, to make that assumption with respect to all
social security recipients without further evidence in support of it, would simply be
speculation, wouldn't it?
MR BROWN: It would be speculation, yes.
MR SCOTT: So would it be right when you first heard about this proposal, you had concerns
about whether it would be lawful?
MR BROWN: Almost immediately my staff, Mr Jones and Mr Lawrence, in discussions with
them, we identified that there was really no way of taking an annualised figure, which is

investigation into what their fortnightly income actually was. So, yes, it was very clear from
our perspective that such a means of determining fortnightly income and, therefore, means
of determining entitlement and debt raising was not supported by the legislation.
MR SCOTT: And when you say you held concerns, may I take it from what you've just said
that you weren't the only one within DSS that held those concerns?
MR BROWN: No. Certainly my team held the same concerns as we discussed it through. We
discussed it with Mr Kimber, so, yes, no, there was - it was not just me.
MR SCOTT: So your team all expressed and expressed agreement with those concerns being
held?
MR BROWN: I recall in particular Mr Jones and Mr Lawrence working on this matter. I had
other team members who were not involved who had sort of very discrete responsibilities
within the team.
MR SCOTT: Okay. And those two other people you have mentioned, they had the same
concerns; correct?
MR BROWN: Yes.
MR SCOTT: Can I just ask that paragraph 30 of your statement be called out and, Mr Brown,
could you just read that to yourself without reading it aloud. And I will ask you something
about it once you've read it to yourself.
MR BROWN: Okay.
MR SCOTT: I'm just going to read the relevant part of that paragraph that I'm going to ask
you about, which is:
"I recall that one of the concerns I had was that the automation policy seemed to have an
analogy to speculative invoicing issues that were being reported in the media in relation to
iiNet v Dallas Buyers Club practices and litigation.”
Do you see that?
MR BROWN: Yes.
MR SCOTT: What do you mean by speculative invoicing?
MR BROWN: Speculative invoicing, that particular context, was where was the notion
that - of course, a lot of illegal downloading was occurring of movies at that particular time,
and other sort of media, and that - which was being discussed in the media and elsewhere.
That people who had downloaded, you know, in particular, that movie, but other movies,
that their IP - ISP addresses, I think they are called - could be given and therefore notices

had illegally downloaded and that this was the penalty for pirating. However, if that
individual settled or paid a certain amount, then the matter would be dropped.
So that's kind of what I - well, that's my understanding of speculative invoicing at that time.
And I felt that there were similarities in this proposal in that the debts would be arrived at in
a manner which was not in accordance with the legislation. Notices would be sent out to
those customers putting the obligation of proof on them, or they could enter into a
repayment agreement with DHS. So I felt there was similarities. At the time, I felt there was
similarities between the practices. They are not exactly the same and, you know, I note that
in terms of illegal downloading, you know, people were actually doing that, whereas in this
particular instance, many, many of those customers would have absolutely done nothing
incorrect.
MR SCOTT: Right. And so you held concerns about the lawfulness of the proposal, correct?
MR BROWN: The lawfulness of the proposal and the sort of ethical basis of it.
MR SCOTT: And it was potentially - indeed, probably - unethical?
MR BROWN: I felt so.
MR SCOTT: Thank you.
COMMISSIONER: Can you expand on that? Why did you think that?
MR BROWN: Well, a lot of the individuals who would end up receiving these notices would
be - the onus of proof on what they earned over the period of time, stretching back
potentially years, would be a level of proof which they simply would not be able to
substantiate. And unemployed people are, almost by definition, they have very vulnerable
cohorts within them, and that there would be people who would enter into agreements to
repay debts, which they had not incurred in the first place, and I felt that the practice as a
result was unethical.
There would, of course, be people who, you know, those debts were legitimate, and there
would, of course, be people who would be able to prove their income within the period.
However, the potential group who DHS were proposing to send these notices to was much
broader. And - but I would note - there was not a lot of detail as to the proposal, and it was
a very initial stage of the proposal, and certainly in policy development it's quite iterative. So
there were, of course, avenues for the proposal to develop and to be more appropriately
targeted as it went through the, you know, development process.
COMMISSIONER: Thank you.
MR SCOTT: Thank you, Commissioner. Now, what this led to - is this right - was that, at your
instigation, your team decided to seek legal advice in relation to the proposal from the
Department's internal legal unit; correct?

MR BROWN: Yes, that's correct. I assume it was at my instigation. Normally an EL1 would
not seek advice on their own. They would need approval. So it was either at my instigation
or just in agreement with Mr Jones and in our discussions that we mutually arrived at that
decision. But I was the Director, so, yes, it would be at my instigation.
MR SCOTT: Alright. And would this be right, that towards the end of October 2014, the
process of drawing instructions to the lawyers for them to provide that advice was in the
works?
MR BROWN: Yes. That's correct.
MR SCOTT: Can we have up on the screen the document from Exhibit 64, which I
understand has been redacted now, which has - ends with the last four digits 0018.
COMMISSIONER: What's the status of this, Mr Scott? Is it an exhibit?
MR SCOTT: It is. It is Exhibit 64.
COMMISSIONER: Thanks.
MS HOGAN-DORAN: Commissioner, could I inquire through my learned friend, in terms of
Exhibit 64, I don't have a bar-coded version. Is he referring to a particular email? Or a
document with a particular date?
MR SCOTT: I am. It's the second email in that bundle, which should have the last four digits
0018.
MS HOGAN-DORAN: And is that an email dated 24 October 2014 at 9.11 am?
MR SCOTT: It is.
MS HOGAN-DORAN: Thank you.
MR SCOTT: I have been told by Deloitte to read out the full number. I apologise.
MR BROWN: Senior Counsel, I don't appear to have that document.
MS HOGAN-DORAN: There is every likelihood that unless Solicitors Assisting have provided
this bundle to Mr Brown that he will have to look at it only on the screen. He won't
physically have it. He doesn't have Exhibit 64.
MR SCOTT: I thank my learned friend. The full document ID should be CTH.9999.0001.0018.
COMMISSIONER: It's up now.
MR SCOTT: Thank you, Commissioner. If you could just scroll down.

COMMISSIONER: This should have turned up in your emails, shouldn't it, Mr Brown?
MR BROWN: Commissioner, I still cannot see the document.
COMMISSIONER: I see. What's the technology behind this, Mr Scott?
MR SCOTT: Perhaps I can blunder on without the document.
COMMISSIONER: Are there likely to be many in this category? Should we be standing down
for 10 minutes to send Mr Brown a few things?
MS HOGAN-DORAN: Commissioner, I'm - could I confer with my friend? Because the
document I thought he was referring to is not this document. The one I said was 9.11 am.
COMMISSIONER: Shall I go away for 10 minutes?
MS HOGAN-DORAN: I'm so sorry, Commissioner.
COMMISSIONER: It's alright.
MS HOGAN-DORAN: We will work together and come with a revised list of documents.
COMMISSIONER: I will just be around the corner. Let me know when you are in good shape
to go.
MR SCOTT: Apologies.
<ADJOURNED 10:40 AM
<RESUMED 10:52 AM
COMMISSIONER: Got a solution?
MR SCOTT: Yes. He now has a screen. Apologies for that, Commissioner. Now, can you see
that document in front of you, Mr Brown?
MR BROWN: Yes, I can.
MR SCOTT: Just for the record, this is taken from Exhibit 64, document ending 008 - sorry,
0018. Can you just confirm that you have read the part of the email from Mark Jones dated
28 October 2014?
MR BROWN: Yes.
MR SCOTT: To Cameron Brown, starting with the words "Hi Cameron" and ending with the
words "Regards, MJ."

MR BROWN: Yes, I can. I can, Senior Counsel.
MR SCOTT: And have you read that?
MR BROWN: Yes, I have.
COMMISSIONER: Can I just reiterate the question I asked you before, should that not have
turned up in the emails provided to you and did it not?
MR BROWN: Commissioner, it did not, and it's pretty clear that I do not have all of my
emails.
COMMISSIONER: Okay. Thank you.
MR SCOTT: And are you satisfied that this email from Mr Jones is setting out proposed or
draft instructions for the legal advice that was under contemplation at this time regarding
the DHS income smoothing proposal?
MR BROWN: Yes, I'm satisfied.
MR SCOTT: Alright. And in the opening words:
"Please find...”
It says "fins" but clearly means find.
MR BROWN: Yes.
MR SCOTT:
"Please find enclosed the request for legal advice."
Does that satisfy you that at some time before this email, there were active discussions
happening regarding getting legal advice from your Department's legal unit about the
proposal?
MR BROWN: Yes, it does.
MR SCOTT: Okay. Can I just ask you about the - some words that appear on the line - the
fourth-last line starting "Happy to discuss." In particular, the words:
"I'm hoping they are worded carefully enough to not immediately put in doubt the evidence
level."
MR BROWN: Yes. Yes.

MR BROWN: Not really the context, but I probably was quite cautious that - the questions
had to be flat and not prefigure the position which we had arrived at. Sometimes where you
request legal advice and where your language is perhaps not sufficiently open or flat
or - you get a very narrow answer. And we really didn't want a narrow answer to this
question. We really wanted to start off with - there are a number of different issues. I think
at the bottom of this document - because I've got - I've got a later iteration of this
document - the questions set out concerns which we had but I wanted those questions to
be flat, not such as, "We believe X is the case. Is X the case?" Because you then just get a
very specific answer.
COMMISSIONER: So you are not a fan of indicating the desired result in your instructions?
MR BROWN: Well, no, not particularly. I would not go so far as to say that I have never done
that. However, certainly not in this case. And it was also - Commissioner, it is - I think it's
important to note that this is very much at the start of the sort of policy formulation
process, and so at the start we are probably trying to find out as much of the surrounding
context and legal context as possible and trying to tease out different issues.
So certainly we were aware that there's complexity in how notices are given, whether a
notice - even whether a notice is actually received, if it's mailed to someone or not received
because they didn't open it. There are a lot of different issues. And we were very keen on
keeping it very open at this particular point in time. And thus the sort of - I think there's six
questions which we sent to our legal area for clarification.
MR SCOTT: Okay. Well, that can be taken down. I'm going to ask you about another
document which I am confident you have. It's document 3 in the bundle of documents that
you have.
MR BROWN: Yes.
MR SCOTT: In the Commission's system, it should be, I think, Exhibit 154 with Doc ID
CTH9999.0001.0026. If that could be brought up. That is CTH.9999.0001.0026. Can you tell
us what this document is, Mr Brown?
MR BROWN: When I received my emails yesterday, attached to them were about - I don't
know, half a dozen to a dozen instant messages. So I think we had a Skype system, and I
think - and this comes from that. So this is Mark - Mr Jones obviously asking me whether we
should go to AGS. There's a sequencing issue with what Mr Jones is saying. You would not
go to AGS before getting formal legal advice from your own internal legal area. And so - - -
MR SCOTT: So this is a - - -
MR BROWN: Sorry, please continue.
MR SCOTT: I didn't mean to cut you off. Please continue.

MR BROWN: So where I'm saying, "Let's see what they say", that's let's see what our people
say.
MR SCOTT: So just to be clear, the subject matter of this conversation record is the question
of who to get legal advice from in respect of the income smoothing proposal from DHS.
MR BROWN: Yes, I only have that fragment, Senior Counsel. I do not have any more.
However, the date, the context, and also me saying black and white tells me that, yes, this is
almost certainly - I would be fully confident that this relates to the legal advice in relation to
income smoothing.
MR SCOTT: Okay. So the first message is from Mr Jones at 2.57 pm on 27 October 2014. It
says:
"Cameron, with this legal advice, do you think there may be a case for going to AGS? The
issues..."
Presumably that means issue:
"...is I believe we have to ask for AGS input rather than Legals going to AGS if they believe it's
appropriate. Otherwise the response back may be to go to AGS.”
Do you see that?
MR BROWN: Yes.
MR SCOTT: AGS, of course, is the Australian Government Solicitor?
MR BROWN: Yes.
MR SCOTT: And the question that is being asked is, instead of going to get internal advice
from the Department's legal unit, whether you just go to the Australian Government
Solicitor instead to get this question answered.
MR BROWN: Yes, that's correct. But typically you cannot go to AGS without going to your
legal area first. It is a sequencing thing. I would also note that, at this point in time, there is

Counsel for the Commonwealth, Mr Begbie, objected to production of 21 documents in
respect of which the issue of public interest immunity arose on the basis that they were said
to be within the class of cabinet documents requiring protection from disclosure. Resolution
of that issue was particularly pressing because of their significance to the evidence to be
given by witnesses in the Commission's first block of hearings.
The Commonwealth relied on material including the affidavit of Ms Leonie McGregor sworn
in respect of documents sought in connection with the class action brought in 2020.
Ms McGregor in that affidavit detailed the basis of the privilege said to apply to
documents - a number of documents, including some of those requiring my consideration
for the purposes of this Commission. In her affidavit, Ms McGregor set out six categories of
documents whose disclosure would be likely to prejudice public interest in the maintenance
of cabinet confidentiality.
Most of the documents under consideration here fell within Ms McGregor's category 2,
"documents which have not been considered by cabinet, but which reveal the contents of
other documents which have been considered by the cabinet or were prepared for
consideration by cabinet", and category 4, "documents prepared by a Department in order
to inform and support cabinet decision-making."
There were three documents which fell into what Ms McGregor nominated as category 1,
which involved documents submitted to cabinet or draft policy papers and preliminary
documents used in preparing documents submitted to cabinet. There was a single
document said to be in category 3, documents prepared by a Department to brief its
Minister for cabinet. There were no documents in category 5, which concerned documents
recording for deliberations and decisions of cabinet, or documents which allowed
reasonable inferences to be drawn in relation to them.
There was not much controversy about the applicable principles. While the class of cabinet
documents clearly attracts a public interest in non-disclosure to ensure that members of
cabinet can deliberate freely with collective responsibility for their decisions and perhaps, to
a lesser extent, to enable candour on the part of public servants in advising their political
masters - and that is a strong interest - it is not absolute. There is a balancing exercise to be

undertaken between the public interest in maintaining their confidentiality and the public
interest in their disclosure.
Mr Begbie emphasised the weight to be given to Ms McGregor's opinion as a very senior
civil servant with extensive experiences in cabinet processes. I accept that her opinion
would not lightly be departed from and that her classifications of documents should be
accepted, but I do observe that where Ms McGregor's schedule did not provide any
information concerning the relevant document which would elucidate the basis of her
classification and/or the connection with her cabinet considerations was not evident on the
face of the document, the potence of the public interest in non-disclosure may be less for
the purposes of the balancing exercise.
Turning to that balancing exercise, fundamental to consideration of the public interest in
production are the Terms of Reference of this Commission. Among other things, I am to
inquire into the establishment, design, and implementation of the Robodebt Scheme and
the Australian Government's responses when the scheme came into question in various
ways. Those Terms of Reference are the government's clear recognition of the powerful
public interest in investigation of how the scheme came to be put into effect and permitted
to continue.
With all of those matters in mind, I turned to consider the 21 documents in respect of which
objection was taken to production. In relation to the three documents in category 1, having
regard to their close connection to the cabinet process, I did not consider that there was a
sufficiently strong public interest for the purpose of this Commission's investigation to
warrant an order for production. Similarly, the single document said to be in category 3 was
not so critical to the Commission's fulfilment of its task as to outweigh the interest in
preservation of its confidentiality.
There was a chain of documents, however, which formed various iterations of the proposals
ultimately sent as a brief to the Minister For Social Services on 12 February 2015, which was
of very great importance to the Commission's task. Because of their significance in exposing
the reasoning and processes leading to the critical brief, which was so fundamental to the
inquiry into the processes and thinking of those behind the scheme, that I considered the
public interest lay in production. That was true of the brief itself also, that the public
interest in its revelations strongly outweighed any interest in confidentiality.
I also order the production of three documents which were briefed to the Minister for
Human Services or his later equivalent, the Minister for Government Services, two of which
were signed by the relevant Minister while one remained in draft form. They were briefs for
noting or information. In relation to two of them, I considered that the public interest
balance lay in favour of removing references to cabinet considerations, including an
